4.4 The Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM)

From the market portfolio to single assets

Section titled “From the market portfolio to single assets”

4.3 The Capital Allocation Line and the Capital Market Line showed that if all investors agree, they all hold the market portfolio (market portfolio) and add the risk-free asset according to their risk aversion. What, then, should the expected return of a single asset be?

For an investor holding the market portfolio, how risky an asset is depends not on its own variance but on how much it adds to the market portfolio’s risk. The market portfolio’s variance is a weighted sum of all pairwise covariances (4.2 Mean–Variance Portfolio Theory), and asset iii‘s contribution is determined by the covariance σiM\sigma_{iM}σiM​ of its return with the market return. Dividing this covariance by the market’s variance gives asset iii‘s beta:

βi=σiMσM2=ρiM σiσM\beta_i = \frac{\sigma_{iM}}{\sigma_M^2} = \rho_{iM}\,\frac{\sigma_i}{\sigma_M}βi​=σM2​σiM​​=ρiM​σM​σi​​

The market portfolio itself has a beta of 1. Beta is also the slope from regressing the asset’s return on the market return (regression coefficient).

In equilibrium, every asset must offer the same reward for the risk it adds; otherwise investors would buy more of the assets with higher rewards and less of the others, and prices would adjust. This gives (Exercises Question 1):

E[Ri]−rf=βi(E[RM]−rf)E[R_i] - r_f = \beta_i \left(E[R_M] - r_f\right)E[Ri​]−rf​=βi​(E[RM​]−rf​)

An asset’s expected excess return equals its beta times the market risk premium E[RM]−rfE[R_M] - r_fE[RM​]−rf​. This is the capital asset pricing model (CAPM), proposed by Sharpe (1964), Lintner (1965) and others.

Check C1
A stock has a very high volatility, but its return has a correlation of 0 with the market return. By the CAPM, its expected return should be:
Would an investor holding the market portfolio bear more risk because of this stock? What does it add to the market portfolio's risk?
What is beta when the correlation is 0? Only a negative beta makes the required return fall below the risk-free rate.
Only an asset with a beta of 1 requires the same expected return as the market.
Check C2
A stock with a beta of 2 must have a volatility exactly twice the market's.
Think: βi=ρiMσiσM\beta_i = \rho_{iM}\frac{\sigma_i}{\sigma_M}βi​=ρiM​σM​σi​​. Besides the ratio of volatilities, what else does beta depend on?

The security market line

Section titled “The security market line”

With beta on the horizontal axis and expected return on the vertical axis, the CAPM is a straight line starting at (0,rf)(0, r_f)(0,rf​) with a slope equal to the market risk premium: the security market line (SML). By the CAPM, every asset should lie on this line.

If an analyst’s expected return for an asset is above the return the security market line requires, the difference is its alpha:

αi=E[Ri]−[rf+βi(E[RM]−rf)]\alpha_i = E[R_i] - \left[r_f + \beta_i\left(E[R_M] - r_f\right)\right]αi​=E[Ri​]−[rf​+βi​(E[RM​]−rf​)]

A positive alpha means that, by the analyst’s expectations, the asset offers more return than its risk requires, so its price is low; a negative alpha means the opposite.

Check C3
In Figure 2-1, raise the market risk premium from 5% to 7%. The alpha of the high-beta stock W:
When the risk premium rises, does the security market line get steeper or flatter? For a stock with a beta of 1.5, does the required return rise or fall?
Alpha is the expected return minus the required return. W's beta is not 0, so its required return changes with the market risk premium.
Check in the figure whether W lies exactly on the new security market line.

Which risk is rewarded

Section titled “Which risk is rewarded”

The capital market line of 4.3 The Capital Allocation Line and the Capital Market Line measures risk by the standard deviation, while the security market line uses beta. They do not conflict: the capital market line applies only to efficient portfolios, while the security market line applies to every asset.

An asset’s risk can be split into two parts: the part that moves with the market, and the company’s own part, unrelated to the market. The latter can be diversified away by holding many assets (diversification); an investor holding the market portfolio does not really bear it, so the market offers no reward for it. Only the part that moves with the market and cannot be diversified away (measured by beta) is rewarded. 4.5 The Single-Index Model and Estimating Beta separates the two parts exactly.

Check C4
Two stocks both have a volatility of 40%. A's beta is 0.5 and B's is 1.5. By the CAPM:
Does an investor holding the market portfolio bear the same risk from both stocks?
Company-specific risk can be diversified away. Does the market reward risk that can be diversified away?
The CAPM's required return needs only beta, the risk-free rate and the market risk premium.

Assumptions, evidence and uses

Section titled “Assumptions, evidence and uses”

The CAPM rests on strong assumptions: investors care only about mean and variance, agree with each other, can all borrow and lend at the risk-free rate, face no taxes or trading costs, and the market portfolio includes all risky assets (including real estate, human capital and so on). None of these holds exactly.

The main empirical findings:

  • The security market line is flatter than the CAPM predicts: low-beta stocks have earned more on average than the CAPM predicts, and high-beta stocks less (Black, Jensen and Scholes, 1972; Frazzini and Pedersen, 2014).
  • Beta does not explain the higher average returns of small-company stocks and stocks with low price-to-book ratios (Fama and French, 1992), which leads to the multifactor models of 4.6 Multifactor Models.
  • The true market portfolio cannot be observed; when a stock index stands in for it, test results depend on the index chosen (Roll, 1977).

Even so, the CAPM remains the model used most in practice: to estimate the cost of equity (cost of equity) and the cost of capital of projects, and to measure fund managers’ performance (4.9 Performance Evaluation). Its most important idea is that only risk that cannot be diversified away is rewarded.

Check C5
If the actual security market line is flatter than the CAPM predicts, then using the CAPM to estimate the cost of equity of a low-beta company gives a result that is too low.
Think: the two lines cross near a beta of 1. At low betas, is the flatter line above or below the CAPM line?

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
  • For an investor holding the market portfolio, an asset’s risk is measured by its covariance with the market: βi=σiMσM2\beta_i = \frac{\sigma_{iM}}{\sigma_M^2}βi​=σM2​σiM​​.
  • CAPM: E[Ri]−rf=βi(E[RM]−rf)E[R_i] - r_f = \beta_i(E[R_M] - r_f)E[Ri​]−rf​=βi​(E[RM​]−rf​); the security market line has beta on the horizontal axis.
  • Alpha is the part of the expected return above what the security market line requires.
  • A company’s own risk can be diversified away and is not rewarded; only the risk that cannot be diversified away, measured by beta, is rewarded.
  • Empirically the security market line is flatter than predicted, and beta does not explain the size and value effects; the CAPM is still widely used to estimate the cost of capital.
